subject: How big models can stan handle?

messages.author: 1c227d73568f2379
messages.subject: How big models can stan handle?
parts:
Hello,

I have an hierarchical model that uses some 360 000 data points and 120 000 variables. I have implemented a Gibbs sampler for it in matlab and now I will make changes to the model and perhaps rewrite it in C++. I would like to use stan in a project but is this a good one? Do you have experience in how big models stan can handle?

BR,
Henrik

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: How big models can stan handle?
parts:
It is mostly a question of how big a model your machine can handle. There are some multivariate models that consume a lot more memory than they should (and some tricks to work around those). There will be some limits on models, once we mere Mike's proposed stuff on RMHMC because of the dense mass matrix. But for NUTS II, I don't think there is any clear limit on the number of parameters, and Marcus has done some models with tens of thousands of parameters.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: How big models can stan handle?
parts:
I've done IRT models that size no problem (I'm not
counting time to get dinner while the model fits
a problem :-)).

The real bottleneck, though, isn't the number of parameters,
but rather the complexity of the expression that computes
the log probability function. That all goes into memory as
an expression graph, and each operation executed takes
24 bytes plus the number of arguments times 8 bytes.

If that number's not too huge, you should be good to go.

- Bob

messages.author: 1c227d73568f2379
messages.subject: Re: How big models can stan handle?
parts:
Update on my quest for bigger models: Now I've hit the limit. The first model i tried, M1, had 360 000 data points and 120 000 parameters. On simulated data it produced one sample per 3 seconds on my desktop computer. For the real data set, performance went down to 56 seconds per sample, which still was acceptable. The results were nice. Then I moved on to catch bigger fish. The second model, M2, had the same data and 300 000 parameters. When ran on a computing server with a AMD Opteron 2435 processor it reserves ~550MB memory and in 18 hours it has produced less than 200 samples of the warm up. This project started as a Gibbs sampler in Matlab, and when I started writing the C++ implementation I tried stan. I guess it's back to the Gibbs then. :)

- Henrik

Henrik,

Did you try the second model with the simulated data set? Have you looked into any reparameterizations? Like the Matt trick (ch. 18 in the reference manual, "Optimizing Stan Code").

Unless the model is really well-behaved, I wouldn't think the estimates from a Gibbs sampler would give you very good results.



Daniel

I'd first check that you're getting effective samples faster
with Gibbs. The issue isn't time per iteration, but time
per effective sample. For instance, check out the examples
in the NUTS paper of Hoffman and Gelman where there are pretty
simple examples that take millions of iterations in Gibbs and
still haven't properly converged. But for some models it'll
work --- depends how much correlation there is in your posterior.

If you send your model, we might be able to help optimize
the code a bit, too.

- Bob
